title: TransFusion: End-to-End Transformer Acceleration via Graph Fusion and Pipelining
problem: Transformer acceleration has focused on fusing individual submodules (MHA, softmax) in isolation, but as models grow in depth and context length, inter-layer data movement, buffer fragmentation, and scheduling inefficiencies across the full encoder/decoder stack (QKV projections, MHA, LayerNorm, FFN) dominate end-to-end latency and cannot be addressed by fragmented per-module optimizations.
motivation: With growing Transformer depth and context lengths, the cross-layer memory traffic and pipeline imbalance between compute-bound FFN and memory-bound attention layers become the dominant performance limiters, requiring an end-to-end view of the full layer stack rather than isolated operator fusion.
method: TransFusion represents the entire Transformer layer stack as Einsum Cascades—a structured graph of mathematical operations that captures which data each operation needs and when it runs. The DPipe scheduler divides this graph and runs different layers in parallel (pipelining), using dynamic programming to find the arrangement that makes FFN and attention stages as fast as possible together. TileSeek, using Monte Carlo Tree Search to explore many random solutions and find good ones, determines how to break computations into chunks on cloud and edge hardware, balancing on-chip memory constraints against data reuse.
key_novelty: Representing the entire Transformer encoder/decoder stack as Einsum Cascades—one mathematical graph—and optimizing inter-layer data movement, intra-layer pipelining, and scheduling end-to-end through dynamic programming (DPipe) and Monte Carlo Tree Search (TileSeek), instead of optimizing each component in isolation.
contributions: Einsum Cascade representation that captures exact data dependencies across the full Transformer stack (QKV, MHA, LayerNorm, FFN)
DPipe: dynamic programming-based scheduler for latency-aware pipelining of Einsum DAG partitions across hardware hierarchies
TileSeek: Monte Carlo Tree Search tiling algorithm that balances buffer reuse and memory budget constraints
Average 1.6x speedup on cloud and 2.2x on edge over state-of-the-art FuseMax by jointly optimizing inter-layer reuse, intra-layer pipelining, and operator scheduling

metrics.speedup: Average 1.6x on cloud, 2.2x on edge over FuseMax

limitations: Not discussed in the abstract; hardware targets are not explicitly named beyond cloud/edge distinctions.
primary_theme: End-to-end Transformer layer fusion and pipelining via Einsum Cascades
